Page 2

Welcome back, explorers

This month is all about one question: is it real, or is it pretend? Pictures, videos and stories can be made by people, by computers, or by both, and it is not always easy to tell.

You do not need to be a scientist to check something. You need a few good questions and the patience to ask them. This paper is full of those questions.

As always, none of the activities need a phone or an account.

Justin Phillips, Editor in Chief, The Guided Planet

Picture: A map of the Guided Planet with its six places joined by a dotted gold path.

Bloop says: I once thought a picture of a cat in a spacesuit was real. It was not. Let's get better at this together.

Page 3 · The Thinking Forest

How to check a picture

Four questions to ask before you believe, or share, a picture you have found.

Picture: A diagram of a machine taking in clues at the top and giving out a guess at the bottom.

Who made it? Look for the name of a person or an organisation you could check.

Where else is it? If something amazing happened, more than one trusted place will usually say so.

Does anything look odd? Hands, writing and shadows are good places to look closely.

How does it make you feel? Pictures made to shock or to rush you deserve a slower look.

Orbit says: My magnifier is enormous, but the best tool is a question.

Hide a mistake

Draw a picture on the grid with one thing wrong in it. Can a grown up spot it?

You need an 8 by 8 grid: draw one with a ruler, eight squares across and eight down.

  1. Draw something simple, like a house or a face.
  2. Add one mistake, like a window in the sky.
  3. Swap with someone and spot each other's mistake.

Colours: Butter, Leaf, Sky, Night.

Page 5 · The Maker District

Design a fake detector

Invent a gadget that helps people check what they see. Start with the person it helps.

Bloop says: Mine beeps when a picture has six fingers. It also beeps at gloves. Work in progress.

My fake detector

Fill in each box and draw big.

  1. Draw it. Draw your detector and label every part.
  2. Who it helps. Who gets fooled, and when?
  3. What it checks. Hands, shadows, writing, where it came from?
  4. What it notices. What clue does it look for?
  5. What it does back. A light, a sound, a message?
  6. Name it. A name worth remembering.
  7. Test it. How would you know it works?

Maker tips

  • Test it on real and pretend pictures you made yourself.
  • A good detector says how sure it is, not just yes or no.

Page 7 · The Connection Garden

Kind words travel too

A kind message can be checked for one thing only: did it make someone's day?

Picture: Two homes on two hills joined by a dotted gold line and a row of flowers.

Checking what is real matters. So does being someone people can trust online. When you share something, you are lending it your name.

If you are not sure something is true, it is fine not to pass it on. Waiting is a kind thing to do.

Pebble says: I turn things the right way round before I share them.

Send a true thing

Write a postcard about something true and good that happened this month.

On the front: Draw the true and good thing. On the back: a message. Post it with a grown up. Or hand it over.

Page 8 · The Thinking Forest

Was this picture made by a computer?

Bloop found a picture of a dog surfing a rainbow. Time for some clues.

Picture: A diagram of a machine taking in clues at the top and giving out a guess at the bottom.

Clue 1: Look at the edges

Are there odd blurs or shapes where things meet?

Clue 2: Look at the details

Hands, teeth, writing and patterns can go wrong.

Clue 3: Look for the maker

Who posted it first, and do they say how it was made?

Clue 4: Look around

Does anyone trusted show the same thing?

Bloop says: Case closed: no single clue proves it. Lots of clues together make a good guess, and a grown up can help you check.

An algorithm is a list of steps for solving a problem.1 Some computers follow steps that make pictures, and some follow steps that recommend what to watch next.2

Try this, no account needed

  • Make a picture yourself, then ask a grown up to guess how you made it.
  • Play Real or Pretend on the next page.

Where this came from

  1. BBC Bitesize, What is an algorithm?
  2. YouTube Help, How YouTube recommendations work

Page 9 · The Thinking Forest

Real or Pretend

One player is the Maker, one is the Detective. Can the Detective tell which cards are real?

Bloop says: I was the Detective and I said everything was pretend. That is not detecting, apparently.

Real or Pretend

Players: 2 to 6. You need: the 12 cards, a pencil, the notebook below.

Set up

  1. Cut out the 12 cards and shuffle them.
  2. The Maker secretly marks some cards REAL and some PRETEND on the back.
  3. Deal three cards face up.

Play

  1. The Detective asks one question about a card.
  2. The Maker answers truthfully.
  3. The Detective says real or pretend, and checks the back.
  4. After round five, swap jobs.

The cards

  • Surfing dog (Animals)
  • Sleeping cat (Animals)
  • Moon base (Space)
  • Rocket launch (Space)
  • Huge goal (Sport)
  • Team photo (Sport)
  • Painted dragon (Art)
  • Clay owl (Art)
  • Robot band (Music)
  • School choir (Music)
  • Giant cake (Food)
  • Pizza face (Food)

Talk about it

  • Which questions helped most?
  • Which cards fooled you, and why?

Going further

  • Make your own cards from pictures you drew yourself.

Page 10 · The Family Explorer

Five good things to explore together

Checked for this issue. Look again together before signing up for anything.

  1. micro:bit MakeCode

    Free, open source block coding for the BBC micro:bit, with a simulator that shows what your program will do.1 New this year: screen reader support for block coding, shaped with blind and low vision young people.2

    Who for: Beginners, with a grown up. Account: Ask a grown up.

  2. Scratch

    Snap code blocks together to make games, stories and animations. Free for everyone.4 Start small: make a cat move, then make it dance.

    Who for: Ages 8 to 163. Account: Ask a grown up first.

  3. ESA Kids

    Space news, facts, animations and downloads from the European Space Agency.5 Liked page 3? Find out more about life in space.

    Who for: Ages 6 to 125. Account: None.

  4. Night sky highlights

    Free guides from Royal Museums Greenwich to what is up in the sky.6 Looking up needs no screen at all. Read it together, then go outside.

    Who for: Everyone. Account: None. Offline: Jot the highlights on paper.

  5. Code Club projects

    Free step by step coding and making guides from the Raspberry Pi Foundation.7 Code Clubs are free for all school aged young people.8 Ask your school or library about a club near you.

    Who for: School aged young people. Account: Not to read the guides.

Orbit says: Same five places as last month, because they are still good. The list changes when something better comes along.

Page 11 · The Family Explorer

Seven days of checking

One small check a day. Tick a circle for everyone who joins in.

Bloop says: Saturday is the best day. You get to fool everyone, kindly.

  1. Monday: Who made it?. Find one picture and work out who made it.
  2. Tuesday: Spot the mistake. Play hide a mistake from page 3.
  3. Wednesday: Ask a question. Ask a grown up how they check things.
  4. Thursday: Invent. Design your fake detector on page 5.
  5. Friday: Send a true thing. Finish the postcard on page 7.
  6. Saturday: Real or Pretend. Play the card game on page 9.
  7. Sunday: Show and tell. Share the best question you asked this week.

On day seven, talk about: Our best question; What fooled us; What we will keep doing.
